item.title: Oprah Winfrey’s Russell Simmons Exit Revisited In Court Letter
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Oprah Winfrey's exit from a Russell Simmons documentary was revisited in a filmmakers' letter reported in his court case.
item.content:encoded:
Oprah Winfrey’s split from the Russell Simmons documentary “On The Record” drew fresh scrutiny after a filmmaker’s letter surfaced in the music mogul’s court fight with Warner Bros. Discovery.

Page Six reported that lawyers for Drew Dixon, the former Def Jam executive who accused Simmons of rape, submitted the letter as an exhibit on October 30.

Its account suggested an unnamed friend’s claims about Dixon may have influenced Winfrey. The filmmakers disputed claims about Dixon’s motives and an alleged romance, writing, “And persons in consensual relationships can be raped.”

Dixon denied a romantic relationship. Simmons denied raping her.

Dixon separately sued Simmons for defamation over his suggestion that her rape allegation was a lie. The letter became public through the case Simmons brought against the documentary’s distributor.

Winfrey withdrew as executive producer before the film’s Sundance premiere in 2020. At the time, she said she “unequivocally believes and supports the women.”

She also said she and the filmmakers did not share a creative vision for telling the women’s stories. Winfrey wanted more reporting and context before the documentary moved ahead. She discussed her withdrawal on “CBS This Morning” in January 2020.

The dispute had also returned to public view in June.

Simmons posted on Threads, hinting at more legal action. No new lawsuit accompanied those comments.

Simmons had already taken his objections to court. In June 2025, he filed a claim in Manhattan Supreme Court against HBO, Warner Bros. Discovery, executive John Stankey and filmmakers Amy Ziering and Kirby Dick. The original filing sought $20 million.

His complaint accused the filmmakers of presenting a one-sided account that harmed his reputation and business.

He contended that interviews, polygraph results and statements favorable to him had been left out. He alleged deceptive business practices and emotional distress, seeking removal of the documentary along with legal fees.

Attorney Imran Ansari argued that continued distribution amounted to republication, making the film’s ongoing availability central to Simmons’ case.

Simmons maintained his denial.

“I am horrified at the false allegations made against me in the Complaint,” he stated. “I do not know and I have never heard of Plaintiff. Her allegation that I committed sexual battery and threatened to rape her son is absurd, shameful, and untrue. I have never had non-consensual sex with Plaintiff or anyone else,” Russell Simmons said.

item.title: Common Performs At El-Sayed’s Final Detroit Rally As Eminem Song Scores Campaign Ad
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Common performed at Abdul El-Sayed's final Detroit rally as Eminem's "Not Afraid" appeared in the Senate candidate's closing ad.
item.content:encoded:
Common performed at Abdul El-Sayed’s final Detroit campaign rally Monday night, while Eminem’s “Not Afraid” appeared in the Michigan Senate candidate’s closing get-out-the-vote video.

The November 2 rally drew at least 650 people to the Majestic Theater. Sen. Elizabeth Warren and other Michigan Democratic leaders joined El-Sayed for his final appeal before the November 3 election.

The Democratic nominee addressed doubts about his chances against Republican Mike Rogers, telling supporters those doubts also sold Michigan voters short.

“And I know Michigan, and I know how big-hearted and open-minded and earnest and gritty, we in this state are,” El-Sayed said.

Common’s appearance was part of a turnout push that asked supporters to do more than attend a show. The campaign’s event listing advertised the Grammy-winning rapper as a special guest for its final Detroit rally and urged people to bring friends, contact family and knock on doors.

“Campaigns aren’t won on TV. They’re won on porches, on sidewalks, in conversations between neighbors who believe Michigan deserves better,” the campaign wrote.

Eminem’s music carried a separate campaign message. El-Sayed’s final campaign video used “Not Afraid,” the rapper’s 2010 single. The ad paired the track with a Michigan-themed message that he was “doing this for MI.”

The song choice also came weeks after Eminem collaborated with Kid Rock on “Heal My Faith.” Kid Rock, a fellow Michigan artist, had compared El-Sayed to the September 11 hijackers, Consequence noted.

Another rapper had already made a campaign appearance for the other side.

Nicki Minaj urged Republican votes at Donald Trump’s October 25 rally at McMorran Place Arena in Port Huron, where she led chants for Rogers and gubernatorial candidate John James.

On October 31, Minaj criticized El-Sayed on X over comments from his October 28 appearance on “Hasan Minhaj Doesn’t Know.” He had discussed his parents missing his high school games and the pressure he felt growing up.

He linked that pressure to learning not to take himself too seriously. Minaj interpreted that account as jealousy and anger directed at white people.

El-Sayed, a former public health official, and Rogers, a former congressman, were seeking the seat of retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters.

item.title: Quando Rondo Leaves Federal Custody After Completing Halfway-House Term
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: Quando Rondo has left federal custody after completing his Atlanta halfway-house term and removing his ankle monitor.
item.content:encoded:
Quando Rondo is out of federal custody after completing the community-confinement portion of his sentence in a marijuana conspiracy case.

The Savannah rapper, whose legal name is Tyquian Bowman, was released from RRM Atlanta on Monday (November 2) and had his ankle monitor removed.

A Facebook post from barber Kwame Bryant, who shared a photo after Rondo stopped by his shop for a haircut.

“I’m glad u finally off paper and out of Federal Custody fam,” Bryant wrote in the post, according to the report.

He also said they played unreleased music during the visit.

The development closes the custody portion of a case that began with Rondo’s December 2023 arrest. He pleaded guilty in August 2024 to conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute and to distribute marijuana.

A federal judge later sentenced him to 33 months in prison, three years of supervised release and a $40,000 fine.

Rondo served roughly 15 months at FCI Edgefield in South Carolina before entering community confinement.

AllHipHop reported in June that he had left the prison for an Atlanta halfway house to complete the final stretch of his sentence.

That distinction matters. Rondo had been out of a federal prison for months, but he remained under Bureau of Prisons custody while assigned to the reentry program.

The Bureau of Prisons says a past release date with no facility listed means a person is no longer in BOP custody, though that person may still be on supervised release or under another authority.

Rondo’s three-year supervised-release term remains part of his sentence. The end of federal custody therefore does not erase the conditions imposed by the court.

The rapper’s projected release date had shifted during the final months of the sentence. Earlier reports listed November 11 before an updated BOP date moved it to November 2.

The new report says that date held and that the monitoring device came off.

Rondo’s release also gives him more room to return to music. The barbershop post indicated that he already has unreleased material in rotation. For now, the concrete change is legal: after moving from prison to community confinement in the spring, he has completed the federal custody phase of the sentence.

item.title: Yella Beezy Defense Uses 17 Other Bookings To Challenge Flight Evidence In MO3 Trial
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Yella Beezy's lawyers pointed to roughly 17 other last-minute bookings as they challenged flight evidence in his MO3 murder trial.
item.content:encoded:
Yella Beezy‘s lawyers used roughly 17 other last-minute flight bookings to challenge the state’s suggestion that his travel around MO3’s killing was suspicious.

American Airlines investigator Diala Alrihani described a frequent traveler during testimony Monday (November 2). She also said entertainment professionals often manage reservations, FOX 4 reported.

The defense pointed to other 2020 reservations made about a day before departure. Those bookings gave jurors a wider view of his travel habits than the trip prosecutors had highlighted.

Airline records placed Yella Beezy and Theodore Thomas on a November 10, 2020 flight from Dallas-Fort Worth to Los Angeles. They booked their return on November 19 and flew back the next day. Some separate reservations had matching booking addresses.

An associate, Devarius Moore, booked a flight from Dallas-Fort Worth to Los Angeles just hours before leaving on November 13, 2020. Records show he returned to Dallas on November 21.

MO3 was killed in Dallas on November 11, 2020. Prosecutors accused Yella Beezy of hiring Kewon White to carry out the shooting. Yella Beezy pleaded not guilty to the charge of capital murder. He also denied hiring White.

White was convicted on September 4 and received a life sentence. Yella Beezy faced a separate jury, with his own freedom at stake.

He could receive life in prison if convicted.

item.title: Flyysoulja Jailed Over $75.45 Walgreens Theft After Overdose
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Flyysoulja was arrested in Broward County over an alleged March theft of $75.45 in goods from a Hallandale Beach Walgreens.
item.content:encoded:
Flyysoulja was arrested in Broward County on November 2 over a $75.45 Walgreens theft police said happened in March.

The Island Boys rapper, whose legal name is Alex Venegas, faced a petty theft charge, Local 10 reported, citing jail records and a Hallandale Beach police report. He had posted bond but was still at Broward County Main Jail as of Tuesday morning, November 3, the station reported.

Police placed the alleged theft on March 20 at the Walgreens on West Hallandale Beach Boulevard. They said video showed him hiding goods in his pants, checking for staff and leaving without paying. The report said he left in a black 2021 BMW. A store manager listed Aquaphor, therapy cream, a razor, Vaseline and lotion.

A witness recognized him from the Island Boys and identified him through a photo, according to the report. Police later obtained an arrest warrant.

Florida’s theft law looks at both value and intent. It covers knowingly taking or using someone else’s property with the aim of depriving its owner of it, even temporarily.

For ordinary property-value cases, Florida classifies theft of goods worth $100 to less than $750 as first-degree petit theft. Grand theft generally starts at $750. The law also sets exceptions for certain property and locations, and prior theft convictions can raise the offense level.

Flyysoulja and twin brother Kodiyakredd reached a mass online audience in 2021 through their poolside video. They turned that viral moment into a recorded song and a music video. Their move from social media to live shows included a booking at Miami’s Club LIV, where the crowd booed their performance.

Separately, Flyysoulja told TMZ he overdosed October 29 and left the hospital November 2.

He had previously discussed his substance use on Instagram Live in November 2025, after a three-day stay at a Miami-area mental health facility.

He said pills had led to an episode in which he damaged his home while broadcasting without realizing it.

“In the psychosis, I was trying to find something for my hair for hours, and destroyed the home while unknowingly being on Live,” he said in that 2025 account.

item.title: Claudia Jordan Takes On Voter Apathy With Warning About Local Power
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Claudia Jordan and Daria Dawson linked voter apathy to local power in a "Morning Hustle" interview ahead of the midterms.
item.content:encoded:
Claudia Jordan had a blunt response for people who tune out politics. On “The Morning Hustle,” she warned that local races carry real power.

“When people say ‘I don’t do politics,’ I’m like, ‘Well, politics will do you,'” Jordan said.

America Votes executive director Daria C. Dawson joined her for the talk. They spoke with host JeremiahLikeTheBible. The interview was published November 2, ahead of the midterms.

Jordan raised concerns about biased judges in Texas, where she lives. She also cited efforts to silence voters there.

Dawson pointed to school boards. Their choices shape what kids learn and school phone rules. She also noted that state election chiefs oversee how the vote is run. Those races, she said, get less press.

She tied efforts to curb voting to a ballot’s worth, asking, “why are they trying to suppress it?”

The pair had taken that message to Atlanta radio days earlier. On October 29, Jordan and Dawson appeared on WAOK’s “Wake Up With Dee Morning Show”. Dr. Dee Dawkins-Haigler hosted the show with Keith Granberry.

“I just need y’all to care,” Jordan said on that show. “If voting wasn’t so important, they wouldn’t be working so hard to take it away from you.”

Jordan also floated a joking “strike” aimed at men who would not vote or act to protect women’s rights. The talk went beyond the push for turnout. It also touched on the need to hold elected leaders to account throughout the year.

Dawson’s group had also put a count on its work. America Votes laid out that work in an October 30 statement. The group said its partners had held more than 5.1 million voter talks this cycle. It said 3.5 million took place face to face at front doors.

The progressive group’s figures covered work in 27 states. That reach went beyond states and races that tend to get the most national press. Its partners worked on races for Congress.

They also took on state and local races. The group said its partners had signed up more than 1.2 million voters nationwide.

“Our partners know their communities. They know how to reach voters,” Dawson said in the statement.

item.title: 50 Cent Faces Tia Kemp Court Delay Over Unserved Papers
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: 50 Cent appeared by Zoom in his Tia Kemp case, but unserved court papers left the next hearing set for December 7.
item.content:encoded:
50 Cent‘s bid for a permanent injunction against Tia Kemp stalled on November 3 because she had not been served, TMZ reported.

He joined by Zoom; Kemp was absent. His side accused her of avoiding service. 50 told the judge he did not want to pursue the matter but felt he had little choice.

The next hearing was set for December 7.

The hearing followed last week’s temporary injunction, which restricted Kemp’s contact with Sire, the rapper’s 14-year-old son with Daphne Joy. The Florida order required her to stay at least 500 feet from the teenager.

It also barred messages sent directly to him or through someone else, including social media posts aimed at him.

The temporary restrictions also covered guns and ammunition. Kemp was required to surrender any weapons after she was served. The earlier order set November 3 for a hearing on whether to impose longer restrictions.

50 had accused Kemp of putting his child into their online feud with posts about Sire’s development. On Instagram, he objected to using a claim about the boy’s health to mock him.

“This is the greatest example of bullying a minor saying he is on the spectrum,” he wrote. Kemp accused him of bullying her in her public response to his legal action.

The protective-order request was one part of a larger court fight. In a separate federal lawsuit, filed October 26 in Los Angeles, the rapper sought at least $6 million on Sire’s behalf. That complaint named the boy as S.J. and accused Kemp of defamation, invasion of privacy and intentional infliction of emotional distress.

His lawyers alleged Kemp invented a diagnosis and made sexually degrading claims about Sire’s mother. They also accused her of continuing to post after receiving a cease-and-desist letter.

“But autism is not shameful,” his lawyers wrote in the complaint.

Kemp’s comments about Sire came after 50 mocked her adult son, William Roberts III. Rick Ross is William’s father.

The dispute involved an alleged assault on William: 50 ridiculed him for seeking police help and again brought Ross’ former job as a correctional officer into their feud.

The Florida case concerned contact restrictions. The federal case sought money over the posts.

item.title: Rhymefest Faces Write-In Challenger In Chicago School Board Reelection
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Rhymefest faced write-in challenger Tameka Walton as his Chicago school board reelection bid reached Election Day.
item.content:encoded:
Rhymefest entered Election Day seeking a four-year term on Chicago’s school board, two years after the rapper won his first seat. The November 3 election puts his work in public education back in front of South Side families.

His District 10a race includes write-in challenger Tameka Walton, a nonprofit director, Chicago Public Schools parent and former Local School Council member. Rhymefest is the only name printed on the ballot after Walton was removed following a petition challenge in July.

The district runs from Bronzeville to South Shore and includes Kenwood Academy and Murray Language Academy.

Chalkbeat’s candidate guide laid out where they differed. The Chicago Teachers Union backed Walton. She opposed school closures and teacher layoffs. Rhymefest questioned how much the Sustainable Community Schools program costs and how well it works.

“The school should be a safe and welcoming space for both the students and the parents,” Walton said in that September profile.

Rhymefest had support from the SEIU Illinois State Council and Common Ground Collective, an anti-CTU political action committee. Reflecting on his 2024 win, he told Chalkbeat, “Money didn’t get me here.”

Born Che Smith, the artist grew up on the South Side.

His campaign biography traced his own school years through Bouchet Elementary, then called Bryn Mawr, and South Shore High School. His son attended Shoesmith Elementary, giving the family another generation of ties to the city’s public schools.

His campaign also pointed to Building Futures. The monthly series brings students, families and school leaders together to discuss education. A second program, Future Builders, gives students a direct line to the board, the campaign said. Both are part of the record he is running on this year.

His interest in reaching young people also came up in a March 2024 AllHipHop interview, before his first school board victory. He spoke about making art for people of all ages. He wanted that work to reach beyond his own needs.

“What our children suffer from is a new type of distraction, which is the technological distraction, which is really the evolution of human beings. You know what I mean? If we can use it as a tool and not be used by the tool,” Rhymefest told AllHipHop.com. “So like I said, this machine, it eats hate…it loves hate. You keep feeding it negativity and hate. However, how can we feed it something else and get a different result and then create something and then see ourselves differently through it.”

item.title: Daddy Yankee Gives Biggie His Flowers For Inspiring Reggaeton
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Daddy Yankee credited Biggie and dancehall on Track Star and said he coined reggaeton's name in 1992, revisiting its roots.
item.content:encoded:
Daddy Yankee credited Biggie and Jamaican dancehall as influences on his music during “Track Star,” where he also claimed he came up with reggaeton’s name in 1992.

During an interview with Jack Coyne, the Puerto Rican star recognized The Notorious B.I.G. and Shabba Ranks as the artists who shaped him. Calling Biggie a formative influence, he said, “he’s a great legend and he inspired me a lot.”

He also named Super Cat, Buju Banton and Beenie Man among the Jamaican artists who influenced Puerto Rican musicians.

Yankee’s claim concerned naming reggaeton. The sound grew out of a wider movement of rappers, DJs and Caribbean music.

A 2023 history published by El País placed Yankee’s use of the word on a DJ Playero recording around 1991 or 1992. Playero recalled the moment as something that happened while they were making a song, rather than a planned announcement of a new genre.

“Nobody knows, neither him nor me. It was part of a song we were putting together,” Playero said when asked why Yankee used the word, calling it “a pure coincidence.”

That history also described an early scene built through cassette sales on Puerto Rican streets. DJ Adam Avilés recalled that the music was called underground before it had a place on radio, television or store shelves.

DJs recorded young rappers over the beats, helping the sound circulate outside the usual industry channels.

Scholar Petra Rivera-Rideau’s essay for the Library of Congress traced underground’s development to Puerto Rican DJs in the early 1990s.

Pioneers such as DJ Negro and Playero “combined sounds from US hip-hop, Jamaican dancehall, and Panamanian reggae en español” with ideas of their own, she wrote.

Yankee had described that connection in his 2007 interview with AllHipHop. Asked whether he considered himself a reggaeton or Hip-Hop artist, he answered, “Both. Both of them.”

“I started it in the Latin world, was as a Hip-Hop artist…Latin Hip-Hop artist. Then, Playero, the reggaeton godfather, introduced me to reggae music and dancehall music. He taught me how to get down [in] the reggae world like 13 years ago, 14 years ago. So thanks to him, I discovered reggaeton music. So I place myself as a Latin Hip-Hop artist and a reggaeton artist, Daddy Yankee told AllHipHop.com.

On “Track Star,” Yankee also credited New York as “the biggest bridge to reggaeton” and identified Héctor Lavoe’s “El Cantante.” “I’m a salsa boy, man, from the heart,” he said.

His own crossover became part of the historical record: “Gasolina,” from his 2004 album Barrio Fino, entered the Library of Congress’ National Recording Registry in 2023. Rivera-Rideau described how the song reached American rap and pop radio, MTV and BET, carrying reggaeton well beyond its early underground audience.

item.title: Positive K Finds A Purpose Bigger Than Rap: Caring For Mom With Alzheimer’s
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Positive K shared how caring for his mother, who has Alzheimer's, changed his life and why caregivers need a team.
item.content:encoded:
Positive K has made caring for his mother his priority as she lives with Alzheimer’s disease.

The rapper discussed looking after his mother, Julie, in an Atlanta News First interview published October 29. She has had the disease for years, with changes to her movement, speech and ability to think.

“This is my assignment in life,” he said.

There have been hard days, but he has also enjoyed choosing outfits for her. He credited the Alzheimer’s Association Georgia Chapter with answering when he sought help from relatives and others.

“It really involves everyone, and that is why you need a team,” Positive K said of caregiving.

He said the experience went beyond music into his personal relationships and changed how he made decisions. He felt he had grown as a son and as a person. He still hoped to return to music full time, taking what he learned from caring for his mother with him.

His creative work has also included stand-up comedy. In a 2023 AllHipHop exclusive, the MC spoke about opening for Mike Epps in 2021 and learning to work different rooms. He described earning his place among comedians rather than relying on his rap fame.

The need for help comes into focus during November, National Family Caregivers Month. The Alzheimer’s Association says nearly 13 million Americans provide unpaid care for someone with dementia. It reports that 59 percent of dementia caregivers experience high emotional stress and 38 percent experience physical stress tied to their care duties.

For families looking for the kind of team Positive K described, the Georgia chapter offers free support groups. Caregivers can join by phone, video or in person, with trained facilitators leading the sessions. There are also groups for people in the early stages of dementia, giving families more than one way to find others facing similar changes.

The association’s free helpline, 800-272-3900, is open around the clock. Callers can speak with someone about local resources or get emotional support and crisis assistance. Conversations are confidential, with bilingual staff and interpreters making help available in more than 200 languages.
